  "content": "# Tamaños y formatos de elementos de DynamoDB

Las tablas de DynamoDB no tienen esquemas, salvo la clave principal. Por este motivo, todos los elementos de una tabla pueden tener atributos, tamaños y tipos de datos distintos.

El tamaño total de un elemento es la suma de las longitudes de los nombres y los valores de sus atributos, además de cualquier gasto adicional aplicable, como se describe a continuación. Puede utilizar las siguientes directrices para calcular el tamaño de los atributos:

- Los valores de tipo String son Unicode con codificación binaria UTF-8. El tamaño de una cadena es *(número de bytes con codificación UTF-8 del nombre de atributo) + (número de bytes con codificación UTF-8)*.
- Los números son de longitud variable, con un máximo de 38 dígitos significativos. Los ceros iniciales y finales se recortan. El tamaño aproximado de un número es *(número de bytes con codificación UTF-8 del nombre de atributo) + (1 byte por cada dos dígitos significativos) + (1 byte)*.
- Un valor binario se debe codificar previamente en formato base64 para poder enviarlo a DynamoDB. Sin embargo, para calcular su tamaño se utiliza la longitud en bytes sin procesar del valor. El tamaño de un atributo binario es *(número de bytes con codificación UTF-8 del nombre de atributo) + (número de bytes sin procesar)*.
- El tamaño de un atributo nulo o booleano es *(número de bytes con codificación UTF-8 del nombre de atributo) + (1 byte)*.
- Un atributo de tipo `List` o `Map` requiere 3 bytes adicionales, independientemente de su contenido. El tamaño de un atributo `List` o `Map` es *(número de bytes con codificación UTF-8 del nombre de atributo) + suma (tamaño de los elementos anidados) + (3 bytes)*. El tamaño de un atributo `List` o `Map` vacío es *(número de bytes con codificación UTF-8 del nombre de atributo) + (3 bytes)*.
- Cada elemento `List` o `Map` también requiere 1 byte de sobrecarga.
- Un conjunto (conjunto de cadenas, conjunto de números o conjunto binario) no requiere ninguna sobrecarga adicional más allá del tamaño de sus elementos. El tamaño de un conjunto es *(número de bytes con codificación UTF-8 del nombre de atributo) + suma (tamaño de valor de elemento)*. Cada valor de elemento se dimensiona según su tipo, con las mismas reglas que el tipo escalar correspondiente, pero sin un nombre de atributo: un elemento de cadena es *(número de bytes codificados en UTF-8)*, un elemento numérico es *(1 byte por cada dos dígitos significativos) + (1 byte)* y un elemento binario es *(número de bytes sin procesar)*.

###### nota

Recomendamos elegir nombres de atributos cortos en lugar de largos. Esto le ayuda a reducir la cantidad de almacenamiento necesario, así como la cantidad de RCU/WCU que utiliza.

A efectos de facturación del almacenamiento, cada elemento incluye una capacidad de almacenamiento adicional por elemento que depende de las características que haya habilitado.

- Todos los elementos de DynamoDB requieren 100 bytes de sobrecarga de almacenamiento por elemento.
- Algunas características de DynamoDB (tablas globales, transacciones, captura de datos de cambios para Kinesis Data Streams con DynamoDB) requieren una capacidad de almacenamiento adicional para tener en cuenta los atributos creados por el sistema como resultado de la habilitación de dichas características. {
  "url": "https://alexdebrie.com/posts/dynamodb-limits",
  "title": "The Three DynamoDB Limits You Need to Know | DeBrie Advisory",
  "content": "Prefer video? [View this post on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nqvlDgnNhPY)!


As a programmer, it is important to know the limits of any service that you're using. In some cases, the limits of a particular service may make it unsuitable for the task at hand, such as [using Route53 as a database](https://www.lastweekinaws.com/blog/route-53-amazons-premier-database/). In other cases, the limit may alter how you structure your solution, such as how the 15 minute limit on Lambda execution time requires you to break down large work into smaller chunks.

In this post, we'll talk about limits in DynamoDB. While the [DynamoDB documentation has a long list of limits for the service](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/Limits.html), most of these are not going to drastically change how you use DynamoDB. For example, nested attributes can only go to 32 levels of depth, I've never found this to be a factor in building my applications.

However, there are a few limits you must understand to model properly in DynamoDB. If you're not aware of them, you can run into a brick wall. But if you understand them and account for them, you remove the element of surprise once your app hits production.

Those limits are:

- [The item size limit](https://alexdebrie.com#dynamodb-item-size-limit);
- [The page size limit for Query and Scan operations](https://alexdebrie.com#page-size-limit-for-query--scan); and
- [The partition throughput limits](https://alexdebrie.com#partition-throughput-limits).

Notice how these limits build on each other. The first is about an individual item, whereas the second is about a collection of items that are read together in a single request. Finally, the partition throughput limit is about the number and size of concurrent requests in a single DynamoDB partition.

In the sections below, we'll walk through each limit, discuss why it exists, and undestand how it affects how you should model in DynamoDB. Finally, we will conclude with some thoughts on [DynamoDB's philosophy of limits](https://alexdebrie.com#the-dynamodb-philosophy-of-limits) and why they're helping you.

Let's get started.

## DynamoDB item size limit[](https://alexdebrie.com#dynamodb-item-size-limit)

The first important limit to know is the item size limit. An individual record in DynamoDB is called an item, and a single DynamoDB item cannot exceed 400KB.

While 400KB is large enough for most normal database operations, it is significantly lower than the other options. [MongoDB allows for documents to be 16MB](https://docs.mongodb.com/manual/reference/limits/#bson-documents), while [Cassandra allows blobs of up to 2GB](https://docs.datastax.com/en/cql-oss/3.x/cql/cql_reference/refLimits.html). And if you really want to get beefy, [Postgres allows rows of up to 1.6TB](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/12/limits.html) (1600 columns X 1GB max per field)!

So what accounts for this limitation? *DynamoDB is pointing you toward how you should model your data in an OLTP database.*

[Online transaction processing (or OLTP)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_transaction_processing) systems are characterized by large amounts of small operations against a database. They describe most of how you interact with various services -- fetch a LinkedIn profile, show my Twitter timeline, or view my Gmail inbox. For these operations, you want to quickly and efficiently filter on specific fields to find the information you want, such as a username or a Tweet ID. OLTP databases often make use of indexes on certain fields to make lookups faster as well as holding recently-accessed data in RAM.

You should have the relevant properties in your database to find the particular record you want. And if the rest of the information for that record is small, you can include that data there as well.

But if you have a large piece of data associated with your record, such as an image file, some user-submitted prose, or just a giant blob of JSON, it might not be best to store that directly in your database. You'll clog up the RAM and churn your disk I/O as you read and write that blob.

Put the blob in an object store instead. Amazon S3 is a cheap, reliable way to store blobs of data. Your database record can include a pointer to the object in S3, and you can load it out when it's needed. S3 has a better pricing model for reading and writing large blobs of data, and it won't put extra strain on your database.

In addition to making you consider the price & performance implications of large blobs, the 400KB item limit also prevents you from making a data modeling mistake.

When modeling data in DynamoDB, you often denormalize your data. For example, in modeling one-to-many relationships, you may [denormalize a collection of child records onto its parent item](https://www.alexdebrie.com/posts/dynamodb-one-to-many/#denormalization-by-using-a-complex-attribute) rather than splitting each child record out into a separate item. This can work well when the number of related items is bounded.

However, if the number of related items is unbounded (think of a customer's orders in an e-commerce store, or a user's tweets in Twitter), then you would want to consider other approaches to model this relationship. Without the item size limit, the access patterns around fetching the parent item would get slower and slower as the size of the denormalized relation grew. By imposing this limit, it forces you to consider the nature of the relationship upfront and [use a different method](https://www.alexdebrie.com/posts/dynamodb-one-to-many/#composite-primary-key--the-query-api-action) if the relationship is unbounded.

In both of these situations, DynamoDB is saving you from reduced performance as your item size grows.

## Page size limit for Query & Scan[](https://alexdebrie.com#page-size-limit-for-query--scan)

While the first limit we discussed involved an individual item, the second limit involves a grouping of items.

DynamoDB has two APIs for fetching a range of items in a single request. The [Query](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/APIReference/API_Query.html) operation will fetch a range of items that have the same partition key, whereas the [Scan](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/APIReference/API_Scan.html) operation will fetch a range of items from your entire table.

For both of these operations, there is a 1MB limit on the size of an individual request. If your Query parameters match more than 1MB of data or if you issue a Scan operation on a table that's larger than 1MB, your request will return the initial matching items plus a `LastEvaluatedKey` property that can be used in the next request to read the next page.

Similar to the second reason for the item size limit, this page size limit forces you to reckon with the performance implications of your data model upfront. [Paginated queries are one of the two areas you might see performance problems as your application grows](https://www.alexdebrie.com/posts/dynamodb-no-bad-queries/#pagination). If you have an access pattern that uses Query *and* could result in more than 1MB of data being looked at, you need to account for pagination in your application code.

Accounting for pagination (by handling the `LastEvaluatedKey` and making follow-up requests) has a great property -- **it's very easy to see understand which areas might slow down as your application grows.**

If I'm doing a PR review and I see `LastEvaluatedKey` being used, my antenna goes up and I know I need to think about implications:

- How likely is it that we'll need to page on this request?
- What are the maximum number of pages we'll need?
- Do we want to allow multiple pages on a single request, or should we push that back to the client?
- Is there another way we can model to reliably reduce request size under 1MB?

The page size also fits in well with DynamoDB Filter Expressions (which you [probably don't want to use](https://www.alexdebrie.com/posts/dynamodb-filter-expressions/)). The 1MB page limit applies *before* the Filter Expression is applied. DynamoDB is teaching us what the expensive parts of an operation are -- finding and reading lots of data from disk.

Contrast this with other database engines. If you're using any [aggregate functions in Postgres](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/9.5/functions-aggregate.html) or [MongoDB's aggregation pipeline](https://docs.mongodb.com/manual/core/aggregation-pipeline/), the code to execute the query can look deceptively simple. But that code is hiding some unknown performance implications under the hood. Aggregations require scanning all of the relevant data. This may be performant when we're talking about hundreds of rows in your test environment, but it will crawl when you hit millions of rows at scale.

## Partition throughput limits[](https://alexdebrie.com#partition-throughput-limits)

We now know how big a single item can be. We know how much data a single request can read. Let's close our discussion of limits with the partition throughput limits, which address how much data *concurrent* requests can handle.

To begin, you need to know some basics around how DynamoDB models its data.

A DynamoDB table isn't running on some giant supercomputer in the cloud. Rather, your data will be split across multiple *partitions*. Each partition contains roughly 10GB of data.

Each item in your DynamoDB table will contain a primary key that includes a partition key. This partition key determines the partition on which that item will live. This allows for DynamoDB to provide fast, consistent performance as your application scales.

For additional background on partitions and how they help DynamoDB scale, check out [Why NoSQL databases can scale horizontally](https://www.alexdebrie.com/posts/dynamodb-no-bad-queries/#why-nosql-databases-can-scale-horizontally).

For an individual partition, there are limits on the maximum throughput you can consume on a per-second basis. You can use up to 3,000 Read Capacity Units (RCUs) and up to 1,000 Write Capacity Units (WCUs) on a single partition per second.

Note -- this is a lot of capacity! This would allow you to read 12MB of strongly-consistent data or 24MB of eventually-consistent data *per second*, as well as to write 1MB of data per second. And remember -- this is per-partition! You can have significantly higher traffic across your table as a whole, and the maximum amount of capacity is effectively unbounded, assuming your credit card is good for it. For many DynamoDB users, they'll never come close to these partitions limits on a full-table basis.

And yet, [some users will blow past 3000 RCUs and 1000 WCUs on a table](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/amazon-prime-day-2020-powered-by-aws/). And this limit helps to guide their data modeling. As you model a high-traffic table, you consider whether you will have partitions that exceed this limit. If so, you can model for it explicitly, whether [using DAX to cache hot items](https://aws.amazon.com/dynamodb/dax/) or by [sharding your partition key to spread the load across your table](https://www.dynamodbguide.com/leaderboard-write-sharding/).

One final note in this area: the DynamoDB team has done a lot of work in the past few years to ensure that the partition throughput limits are the only thing you need to consider when thinking about traffic across your table.

In the old days of DynamoDB (pre-2018), DynamoDB would spread your provisioned throughput equally across all partitions in your table. This could lead to issues if your workload was unbalanced. Imagine you had certain keys that took more traffic than others -- think of the distribution of popular tweets or Reddit threads. Because the throughput is spread equally, you could be getting throttled in one partition while you had capacity to burn in others.

This led to DynamoDB users needing to overprovision their tables to account for their hottest partitions rather than for overall traffic. By extension, you needed to care about two things: the partition throughout limit as well as your hottest partitions.

DynamoDB changed that with [adaptive capacity](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/database/how-amazon-dynamodb-adaptive-capacity-accommodates-uneven-data-access-patterns-or-why-what-you-know-about-dynamodb-might-be-outdated/). Adaptive capacity works by spreading your provisioned throughput across your table according to demand rather than spreading it evenly. If you have one partition taking more traffic, it will take capacity from one of your other partitions.

Initially, adaptive capacity would take 5 - 30 minutes to spread capacity across your table. In May 2019, [adaptive capacity became instant](https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2019/05/amazon-dynamodb-adaptive-capacity-is-now-instant/), meaning you could have highly variable workloads from one second to another, and DynamoDB would spread your capacity accordingly.

There are two major implications of adaptive capacity. First, for all users, this meant less that you needed to think about. You don't need to do the math to calculate the number of partitions in your table as well as the required throughput to give enough capacity to your hottest partition. You only need to consider overall throughput when doing capacity planning.

Second, this opened up some data modeling patterns for tables with lower traffic. Generally, [you want to spread your data evenly across your partitions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/bp-partition-key-uniform-load.html). However, this can make it harder to do queries that look at your entire table, such as finding all entities of a particular type or finding the top N items in the dataset.

If you won't go anywhere near the partition throughput limits, you can create large partitions that handle these access patterns. You need to be absolutely sure you won't hit them -- otherwise you're in for a nasty surprise at some point -- but it can make it easier to handle these patterns.

## The DynamoDB philosophy of limits[](https://alexdebrie.com#the-dynamodb-philosophy-of-limits)

In the sections above, we've seen how these key limits are designed to point you in the proper direction for modeling your data. But they're doing more than that -- they're reducing the complexity of understanding your database performance.

With traditional databases, your performance is on a spectrum. The response time for a query can vary significantly based on a number of factors -- size of the dataset, the hardware running your database (including CPU, RAM, disk, and network bandwidth), and the other queries running at the same time.

This variability makes it very difficult to plan how your application will perform as it scales. Load tests that simulate actual traffic are difficult, particularly for a new service, so you may just roll something out there and pray for the best.

With DynamoDB, performance isn't a spectrum. It's binary -- yes or no. You know the exact limits where your access patterns won't work anymore, whether it's due to pagination on your Query or throttling on your hot keys.

These limits surely aren't the absolute maximum that DynamoDB can handle. We know that DynamoDB *could* handle items over 400KB -- after all, they're handling 1MB of data in Query & Scan operations!

And we know that DynamoDB *could* handle more than 1MB on a Query or Scan operation, as the [BatchGetItem operation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/APIReference/API_BatchGetItem.html) can return up to 16MB of data.

Finally, I'm sure DynamoDB could go beyond 3000 RCUs or 1000 WCUs on a single partition if it really wanted to push it.

But the key is that DynamoDB is drawing a line and guaranteeing performance everywhere before that line.

Your database has physical limits. If you don't know what they are, you're flirting with danger. I've personally experienced issues with Elasticsearch under high load where everything is going swimingly, then the entire database falls over suddenly and without warning. In Postgres, you might [lock up your database with multi-transactions](https://buttondown.email/nelhage/archive/notes-on-some-postgresql-implementation-details/). And don't get me started with MongoDB's aggregation framework.

The more I work with other databases, the more I prefer the explicit limits of DynamoDB as compared to the unstated limits of other tools.

## Conclusion[](https://alexdebrie.com#conclusion)

In this post, we covered the three limits that matter in DynamoDB. First, we saw the limit of an individual item. Next, we looked at the page size limit for Query and Scan operations. Then, we saw how the partition throughput limit regulates concurrent access to certain items.

Finally, we closed with some thoughts on how the DynamoDB limits are helping you. With most databases, performance is on a spectrum with a number of often-unknowable factors combining to determine your response time. With DynamoDB, performance is binary -- as long as you fit within the limits, your performance is knowable.

If you have questions or comments on this piece, feel free to leave a note below or [email me directly](mailto:alexdebrie1@gmail.com).",

  "url": "https://dynobase.dev/dynamodb-limits",
  "title": "DynamoDB Limits: Item Size, API Limits and Quotas",
  "content": "DynamoDB's maximum item size is **400 KB**, including attribute names and values. Query and Scan evaluate at most **1 MB per page**, batch writes accept **25 operations**, and transactions cover at most **100 distinct items and 4 MB**. These fixed constraints are separate from adjustable defaults such as **20 GSIs per table** and **40,000 read or write units per second per table or GSI**.

The tables below cover items, keys, indexes, operations, throughput, control-plane requests, Streams, backups and vector search. Values are checked against the AWS [service quotas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/ServiceQuotas.html) and [constraints](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/Constraints.html) documentation. DynamoDB uses binary size units: 1 KB is 1,024 bytes, so 400 KB is 409,600 bytes.

## Fixed limits versus adjustable quotas

A **fixed constraint** requires a data-model or application change. AWS cannot raise the item-size limit or make a transaction contain more items. An **adjustable quota** is an account setting: check the applied value for the correct Region in Service Quotas before treating the published default as your ceiling.

In the tables, **Service Quotas** identifies quotas you can request there. **AWS Support** identifies increases or allowlisting routed through support. **Fixed** means design around the value. Where AWS publishes a default without documenting self-service adjustment, the table says so rather than promising an increase.

## Items and attributes

| Constraint | Limit or rule | Adjustable? | 
|---|---|---|
| Maximum item or record size | 400 KB, including attribute names and values | Fixed | 
| String and Binary attribute size | Must fit within the item's 400 KB total | Fixed | 
| Attributes per item | No separate count limit; the entire item must fit | Fixed size constraint | 
| List, Map or Set elements | No separate count limit; the entire item must fit | Fixed size constraint | 
| Nested document depth | 32 levels | Fixed | 
| Number precision | 38 significant digits | Fixed | 
| Positive Number range | `1E-130` through `9.9999999999999999999999999999999999999E+125` | Fixed | 
| Negative Number range | `-9.9999999999999999999999999999999999999E+125` through `-1E-130`; zero is also valid | Fixed | 
| General attribute name size | At least one character and less than 64 KB; use 65,535 bytes as the upper bound | Fixed | 
| Key attribute names | 1 to 255 characters in the key-schema APIs; index key names must also fit 255 UTF-8 bytes | Fixed | 
| User-specified projected attribute names | `NonKeyAttributes` accepts names up to 255 characters; keep names within 255 UTF-8 bytes | Fixed | 
| Empty values | Empty Strings and Binary values allowed outside table/index keys; empty Lists and Maps allowed | Fixed rules | 
| Sets | Nonempty, unique elements of one type: String, Number or Binary; no order guarantee | Fixed rules | 
| Item with local secondary indexes | Base item plus its corresponding LSI entries must fit the documented 400 KB combined limit | Fixed | 

An empty set is invalid even though an empty list is valid. Empty String and Binary elements can appear inside sets, lists and maps. `NULL` is a supported attribute type; it is different from an absent attribute and cannot be a key.

### How DynamoDB counts item size

Count the UTF-8 bytes of every attribute name, plus its value's stored representation. Multibyte characters can use more space than their character count suggests. Binary data is counted using its decoded length, although its base64 wire representation is larger. Numbers use DynamoDB's numeric representation, not simply the length of their JSON text.

Lists and maps add 3 bytes of container overhead and 1 byte per element, in addition to names and nested values. Booleans and nulls use 1 byte plus the attribute name. AWS's [item-size calculation rules](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/CapacityUnitCalculations.html) distinguish this item data from the additional storage overhead used for billing. Do not use the length of `JSON.stringify(item)` as an exact size validator.

Use the [item size and capacity calculator](https://dynobase.dev/dynamodb-capacity-and-item-size-calculator/) when choosing how much data to keep together. Size also affects cost: writes round up in 1 KB units, and reads in 4 KB units. The 400 KB limit is a maximum, not a recommended item size.

## Partition keys and sort keys

| Constraint | Limit or rule | Adjustable? | 
|---|---|---|
| String/Binary partition-key value | 1 to 2,048 bytes | Fixed | 
| String/Binary sort-key value | 1 to 1,024 bytes | Fixed | 
| Key attribute types | String, Number or Binary; no Map, List, Set, Boolean or Null keys | Fixed | 
| Base-table primary key | One partition-key attribute, with one optional sort-key attribute | Fixed | 
| Multi-attribute GSI keys | Up to 4 partition-key and 4 sort-key attributes | Fixed | 
| Distinct partition-key values | No practical count limit | No count quota | 
| Distinct sort-key values under a partition key | No practical count limit, subject to item-collection constraints with LSIs | No count quota | 

The key-length limits concern **values**, not the length of attribute names. Number keys follow the Number range and precision rules. For multi-attribute GSIs, use the documented composite-key constraints rather than assuming the base-table key layout applies unchanged.

## Table and index quotas

| Resource or operation | Default or limit | Adjustable? | 
|---|---|---|
| Tables per account per Region | 2,500 | Service Quotas/account team; documented maximum 10,000 per account per Region | 
| Total table size and item count | No practical limit | No size/count quota | 
| Global secondary indexes per table | 20 | Service Quotas | 
| Local secondary indexes per table | 5 | Fixed | 
| Explicit `INCLUDE` attributes across all indexes | 100 total; the same name in two indexes counts twice | Fixed | 
| `NonKeyAttributes` per index projection | 20 | Fixed | 
| LSI item collection | 10 GB for all base-table items and projected LSI entries sharing a partition-key value | Fixed | 
| Adding GSIs with `UpdateTable` | One new GSI per operation | Fixed operation constraint | 
| Creating tables with secondary indexes | Serialize creation; AWS documentation conflicts on concurrent indexed-table counts | See note below | 
| Table and secondary-index names | 3 to 255 characters: letters, digits, underscore, hyphen or dot | Fixed | 
| Table name uniqueness | Within an account and Region | Fixed | 
| Index name uniqueness | Within its base table | Fixed | 

The 100-attribute projection quota does not apply to `ALL` or `KEYS_ONLY`. Automatic projection of table and index keys does not use the user-specified projection allowance. The separate per-index limit comes from the [Projection API](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/APIReference/API_Projection.html).

LSIs must be created with the table and cannot later be added or removed. GSIs can be added later, but a new index is not queryable until it becomes `ACTIVE`. Follow the [online index creation rules](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/GSI.OnlineOps.html), and serialize table creation where secondary indexes are included. The CreateTable introduction says only one indexed table can be in `CREATING`, while its error description mentions up to 250 concurrent indexed-table creations. Because those statements conflict, do not rely on either as an unconditional current quota.

### Is DynamoDB limited to 10 GB?

No. The **10 GB item-collection limit applies to tables with LSIs**, not to the whole table. It includes the base-table data and LSI projections for one partition-key value. Without LSIs, an item collection can be split across physical partitions. A partition key that accumulates an unbounded history is therefore a particular risk when you choose an LSI.

## Data operations and request sizes

| Operation | Limit | Application behavior | 
|---|---|---|
| `GetItem`, `PutItem`, `UpdateItem`, `DeleteItem` | One item per call; stored item maximum 400 KB | An update must also leave a valid-sized item | 
| `Query` | Up to 1 MB evaluated per call, before filtering | Continue with `LastEvaluatedKey` | 
| `Scan` | Up to 1 MB evaluated per call, before filtering | Continue with `LastEvaluatedKey` | 
| Parallel `Scan` | `TotalSegments` from 1 to 1,000,000 | Keep each segment's continuation key with that segment | 
| `BatchGetItem` | Up to 100 items and 16 MB returned; may return partial results above 1 MB per partition | Retry `UnprocessedKeys` | 
| `BatchWriteItem` | Up to 25 puts/deletes and 16 MB request payload | Retry `UnprocessedItems` | 
| `TransactWriteItems` | Up to 100 distinct items and 4 MB aggregate item data | All actions succeed or fail together | 
| `TransactGetItems` | Up to 100 distinct items and 4 MB aggregate item data | Atomic read, without index access | 
| PartiQL `ExecuteStatement` | Statement length up to 8,192 characters; reads evaluate up to 1 MB or `Limit` items | Follow returned `NextToken` | 
| PartiQL `BatchExecuteStatement` | Up to 25 statements | All reads or all writes; check individual errors | 
| PartiQL `ExecuteTransaction` | Up to 100 statements, within transaction item and size limits | Reads or writes, not a mixed transaction | 

The [BatchGetItem API](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/APIReference/API_BatchGetItem.html) can return a successful response with unprocessed keys. Likewise, [BatchWriteItem](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/APIReference/API_BatchWriteItem.html) can return unprocessed operations. Retry only those entries with exponential backoff and jitter. Batches are not transactions, and batch writes do not support updates or per-item conditions.

The wire payload can exceed stored item size because of DynamoDB JSON type wrappers and base64 encoding. A batch must satisfy both the item-level constraints and the total request limit.

A `TransactWriteItems` idempotency token remains valid for 10 minutes after the first request completes. Reusing it with different request parameters during that window fails; after the window, the request is treated as new.

Transactions cannot contain two actions on the same item, including a `ConditionCheck` plus an `Update`. Attach the condition to the update instead. They must stay within one account and Region. An MREC global table does not replicate a transaction atomically to other Regions, and MRSC global tables do not support transactions. See the [transaction guide](https://dynobase.dev/dynamodb-transactions/) for patterns that preserve the required atomic boundary.

PartiQL is another API surface over the same database constraints. Its [statement](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/APIReference/API_ExecuteStatement.html), [batch](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/APIReference/API_BatchExecuteStatement.html) and [transaction](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/APIReference/API_ExecuteTransaction.html) limits do not make SQL-style joins or arbitrary cross-item updates available.

## Expression limits

| Expression component | Limit | Adjustable? | 
|---|---|---|
| Each expression string | 4 KB | Fixed | 
| Single substitution token such as `#name` or `:value` | 255 bytes | Fixed | 
| Combined `ExpressionAttributeNames` and `ExpressionAttributeValues` substitutions | 2 MB | Fixed | 
| Operators/functions in an expression | 300 | Fixed | 
| Operands in an `IN` comparison | 100 | Fixed | 
| Document-path dereferences | 32 | Fixed | 

The 255-byte substitution-token limit does not mean every String value stored through an expression is limited to 255 bytes. Account for the combined substitution size separately.

The 300-operator limit applies to condition, filter and update expressions. Comparators, logical keywords, functions and arithmetic operators count. In `SET price = price + :delta`, the `+` counts; the assignment `=` does not. Reserved attribute names remain usable through `ExpressionAttributeNames` aliases.

## Throughput and partition limits

| Scope | Provisioned mode | On-demand mode | Adjustable? | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Physical partition | 3,000 read units/s and 1,000 write units/s | Same | Fixed partition capability | 
| Table or individual GSI | 40,000 RCU and 40,000 WCU | 40,000 RRU/s and 40,000 WRU/s | Service Quotas | 
| Account, per Region | 80,000 RCU and 80,000 WCU across provisioned tables and GSIs | No account-level aggregate read/write quota | Service Quotas for provisioned quotas | 
| Minimum provisioned table/GSI capacity | 1 RCU and 1 WCU | Not applicable | Published minimum | 
| Provisioned table with Streams enabled | Default 40,000 WCU write quota | Not applicable | Service Quotas | 
| Switch from provisioned to on-demand | Up to 4 times per rolling 24 hours | Destination mode | Fixed switching rule | 
| Switch from on-demand to provisioned | Destination mode | At any time | Subject to table operation state | 
| Provisioned decreases | Up to 27 per UTC day for each table/GSI | Not applicable | Service Quotas | 

Units are not interchangeable with request counts. A strongly consistent read of up to 4 KB uses one read unit, an eventually consistent read uses half, and a transactional read uses two. A write of up to 1 KB uses one write unit, or two for a transaction.

The decrease quota starts with four available decreases at the beginning of the UTC day. One replenishes each hour, with at most four available at once. This allows 27 decreases across a full day. Tables and GSIs have independent allowances, but an update decreasing both fails if either has exhausted its allowance.

An on-demand table can also have a user-configured maximum throughput target. That is separate from its service quota and **warm throughput**, which describes throughput it can handle immediately. Increasing a quota does not fix a hot key or automatically pre-warm a table. Inspect the resource ARN and `ThrottlingReasons` before changing capacity; the [throttling guide](https://dynobase.dev/dynamodb-throttling/) explains each limit category.

## Control-plane API quotas

These APIs create or describe resources. Their quotas are independent of item read/write capacity and generally apply per account per Region. The AWS constraints page does not mark every API rate as adjustable through Service Quotas, so do not assume a throughput quota increase raises them.

| API or group | Published rate or concurrency constraint | 
|---|---|
| `CreateTable`, `UpdateTable`, `DeleteTable`, `PutResourcePolicy`, `DeleteResourcePolicy` | Default 500 combined operations in flight, adjustable through Service Quotas; separate operation-specific limits still apply | 
| Mutable control-plane group above | 2,500 requests/s combined, with lower individual policy limits | 
| `DescribeTable`, `ListTables`, `GetResourcePolicy` | 2,500 requests/s combined | 
| `PutResourcePolicy` | 25 requests/s; wait 15 seconds after a successful policy update before another on that table | 
| `DeleteResourcePolicy` | 50 requests/s; blocked for 15 seconds following a successful policy put on that table | 
| `GetResourcePolicy` | 100 requests/s | 
| Resource-policy document | 20 KB, including whitespace | 
| `DescribeLimits` | Call at most once per minute to avoid throttling | 
| `DescribeStream` | 10 requests/s | 
| `DescribeTableReplicaAutoScaling`, `UpdateTableReplicaAutoScaling` | 10 requests/s each | 
| `DescribeContributorInsights`, `ListContributorInsights`, `UpdateContributorInsights` | 5 requests/s each | 
| `DescribeTimeToLive` | 10 read request units/s | 
| `UpdateTimeToLive` | One enable/disable request per table per hour | 
| `CreateBackup` | 50 requests/s | 
| `DescribeBackup`, `DeleteBackup` | 10 requests/s each | 
| `ListBackups` | 5 requests/s |

A resource policy adds weight to mutable request accounting: two extra requests per KB of policy. For example, creating a table with a 5 KB policy counts as 11 requests. Deployment tooling should use bounded concurrency and backoff rather than retrying every resource at once. Backup API rates are documented in [CreateBackup](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/APIReference/API_CreateBackup.html), [DescribeBackup](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/APIReference/API_DescribeBackup.html), [DeleteBackup](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/APIReference/API_DeleteBackup.html) and [ListBackups](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/APIReference/API_ListBackups.html).

## Workarounds for the limits people hit most

### Items larger than 400 KB

Store large binary objects or documents in S3 and keep their object key, metadata and version in DynamoDB. Alternatively, split a document into separately addressable items, or compress a payload that does not need attribute-level querying. Leave space for keys and future attributes. Compression removes the ability to filter the compressed content directly, and splitting creates a multi-item consistency problem you must handle explicitly.

### Query or Scan results larger than 1 MB

Keep requesting pages using the returned `LastEvaluatedKey` as `ExclusiveStartKey`. A filter runs after DynamoDB evaluates a page, so an empty `Items` array is not an end-of-results signal. Continue until there is no continuation key. The [pagination guide](https://dynobase.dev/dynamodb-pagination/) covers the implementation.

An API `Limit` counts evaluated items, not matches after filtering. If most evaluated data is discarded, fix the key condition or index rather than issuing larger scans. DynamoDB does not provide SQL joins, arbitrary ordering or offset pagination; its query shape follows the key design.

### Transactions larger than 100 items or 4 MB

First reduce the atomic unit: keep the small set of records that must change together in one transaction. Move large immutable payloads elsewhere. If a workflow must span several transactions, use explicit progress records, idempotency and compensating actions. Splitting a transaction into batches does not preserve all-or-nothing behavior.

### Hot partitions despite spare table capacity

[Find the hot key](https://dynobase.dev/dynamodb-hot-partitions/) and determine whether reads or writes are throttling. Cache repeated reads when staleness is acceptable, distribute writes across a suitable key space, or shard a write-heavy aggregate and combine results on read. Adaptive capacity and splitting help distribute load, but a single hot item still has a partition's limits. An LSI also prevents splitting an item collection across partitions.",
